I am told it can rewrite the spells of life.”

“Parts of them,” said Mira, the council’s geneticist. “And the parchment matters. Every living cell carries DNA, a long set of instructions. Changes in those instructions can influence how an organism grows, functions, or develops disease.”

“So CRISPR is an enchanted quill?”

“Think of a guide and a pair of molecular scissors. A short piece of RNA guides a protein—often Cas9—to a matching stretch of DNA. The protein cuts there. Then the cell’s own repair machinery takes over.”

Archmage Thorne leaned forward. “And repairs it exactly as we command?”

“Sometimes,” Mira replied. “We can disrupt a gene or, under suitable conditions, supply a template for a specific change. But repair is not perfectly predictable. Newer tools, called base editors and prime editors, can make certain changes without cutting both strands of DNA.”

The healer unrolled a scroll. “What good can these instruments do?”

“Already, considerable good. Some approved treatments edit a patient’s blood-forming stem cells to treat sickle cell disease and certain cases of beta thalassemia. For sickle cell disease, one approach restores production of fetal hemoglobin, helping prevent red blood cells from sickling.”

“Then we can cure every inherited illness!” declared Thorne.

Mira raised an eyebrow. “A splendid proclamation. A poor medical forecast. Some diseases involve one well-understood gene; others involve many genes, the environment, and chance. Even when we know what to change, delivering the editor safely to the right cells can be difficult.”

The keeper of the gardens spoke next. “And beyond healing?”

“Researchers use CRISPR to learn what genes do, investigate diseases, and develop treatments. In agriculture, it can help produce crops with traits such as disease resistance or tolerance of difficult growing conditions. Every application still needs testing: a useful edit does not guarantee a healthy organism or a harmless ecological outcome.”

“And the dangers?” asked the High Wizard.

“The scissors may act at unintended sites. Even the intended site can undergo unwanted changes. Some cells may receive the edit while others do not. We must examine safety, durability, and effects on the whole organism.”

A young wizard lifted a glittering catalogue. “Stronger children? Greater intelligence? Wings?”

“Put the catalogue away,” said the healer.

“Complex traits are not single spells,” Mira explained. “They involve many interacting factors. Editing embryos or reproductive cells also raises special concerns: changes could be inherited by future generations, who cannot consent. That differs from editing a patient’s body cells, which generally does not pass the changes to their children.”

The treasurer cleared his throat. “Who can afford such magic?”

“An essential question,” said Mira. “A treatment’s scientific success does not ensure fair access. Cost, specialist care, informed consent, and public oversight all matter.”

The High Wizard closed the meeting book.

“Then let the record show: CRISPR gives us a powerful way to study and alter life’s instructions. Its promise is real, its precision has limits, and wisdom must accompany its use.”

“And no wings?” whispered the apprentice.

“Not in this year’s budget,” said the treasurer."}
